sentences.text: Leedsichthys was an extinct genus of fish belonging to the pachycormid family, which lived in oceans during the Middle to Late Jurassic.
Most of its body was made of cartilage that rarely preserved, yet over seventy partial individuals have been recovered, revealing toothless jaws.
This animal holds the record for the largest known member of the bony fish lineage.
Arthur Smith Woodward named the genus in 1889, honoring British collector Alfred Nicholson Leeds.
The type species is Leedsichthys problematicus, while a second species named in 1999 from Chile was later deemed indistinguishable from it.
Remains have been found in England, France, Germany, Argentina, and Chile, specifically within the Callovian, Oxfordian, and Kimmeridgian stages.
It fed mainly on plankton by filtering seawater with gill rakers equipped with delicate bone plates to catch zooplankton and small animals.
Scientists are still unsure whether algae or phytoplankton were part of its diet.
Growth rings in its remains suggest it took between 21 and 25 years to reach adult size.
Leedsichthys was part of a lineage of large filter-feeding fish that existed from the Middle Jurassic until the end of the Cretaceous.
Researchers debate whether Pachycormidae, including Leedsichthys, are basal Teleostei or belong to a separate order sister to Teleostei.
Fossils of this fish range from the Callovian to the Tithonian stages.
A scientific debate exists regarding the animal's size, with Liston arguing for much lower length estimates than earlier popular accounts.
In 2010, Liston also suggested that furrows in Swiss sea floors were made by Leedsichthys spouting water to eat bottom-dwelling animals, rather than by plesiosaurs.

Martill proposed in 1999 that climate change at the end of the Callovian caused extinction in northern seas, with the southern Ocean as a refuge, but Liston countered in 2010 by noting fossils from the Kimmeridgian in Normandy.
